feedback.text:
It is good to learn more about your personal situation. Based on that, we can offer you some suggestions for chapters, that might be especially relevant for you. They are highlighted in green colour on the scroller page.

Of course, you are welcome to explore all the other chapters as well!

main.text: Below, you can see the topics that are most relevant for your personal journey. To access these contents, click on ‘Continue’ and start each chapter from the overview page.

text-1.1: Meeting an Old Friend
text-1.2: Imagine you are visiting the kopitiam after accompanying your loved one for a doctor’s appointment.
text-1.3: While queuing for food, you start scrolling through your work emails to catch up and begin thinking about the next thing on your list.

text-2.1: Helping Hands Are All Around
text-2.2: You are not sure why, but what Adam said stays with you, Part of you shrugs it off. Another part wonders if there is something you are missing.
text-2.3: You browse through the brochure and a quote by Adam from the article catches your eye:

quote-1.quote: I don't think I'm the best person, but what to do? She's my mother and she needs me now, so I just take things one step at a time.

item-1.1: Many people become caregivers to their parents, spouses, children or other loved ones. They are managing every aspect of care and sometimes may feel overwhelmed by the weight of their responsibilities.

text-4.1: Something in the brochure makes you pause – it feels like someone truly understands what you’re dealing with. Maybe you’re not the only one facing this after all. You take a closer look, hoping to find that small bit of help you need.

back.1: … you are providing financial or emotional support for your loved one.
… you are managing your loved one’s activities of daily living, such as showering or performing household tasks.

text-6.1: Caring for your loved one needs time and resources. There can be many reasons why they depend on you. They may be frail or elderly, experience mental health conditions (such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or depression) or serious physical illness (like cancer, stroke, dementia etc.).

text-7.2: Caregiving isn’t a one-sided experience. While you provide care and support, your loved one also impacts you. Most of the time both of you will face challenges together in a dynamic relationship.
text-7.3: What you’re about to learn uses real-life caregiving stories to highlight how caregiving can affect both the person receiving care and the person providing it.
text-7.4: Let’s take a look at Adam’s caregiving journey – from the time he became a caregiver to how he became a mentor for other caregivers.

p1.1: When he found out about his mother's heart failure, ...
p1.2: ... Adam was filled with worry and had trouble sleeping at night.

p2.1: Adam was consumed by managing his mother’s care – scheduling medical appointments, organising medication, and taking her for tests. Without realising it, he stopped playing badminton, something that once brought him joy. It wasn't just his schedule that was full - his mind was too.

p3.1: He was also too exhausted to join his friends for their usual makan sessions.

p4.1: He spent most of his time with his mother and started feeling lonely and isolated.

order-1.title: Take a moment and reflect: Which aspects of your life are most affected by caregiving?

correct.2: There is no single right way to approach caregiving. It depends on your situation, your priorities and your needs. Taking time to reflect can help you identify what feels manageable for you and where additional support may be helpful.
correct.3: The next section introduces care management – a set of approaches and resources that can support you along the way.

incorrect.2: There is no single right way to approach caregiving. It depends on your situation, your priorities and your needs. Taking time to reflect can help you identify what feels manageable for you and where additional support may be helpful.
incorrect.3: The next section introduces care management – a set of approaches and resources that can support you along the way.

reveal-1.locked: Reflect on the influence on your life to proceed.

row-2.1: There is no one-fits-all approach to cope with your limited time, but …
row-2.2: … you can find ways to manage negative emotions, cope with emotional burdens and care for yourself here (opens in new tab).

text-8.2: A healthy caregiving relationship involves both sides appreciating each other’s roles, sharing responsibilities, and seeing caregiving as more than a duty – it is an opportunity to connect and support each other’s well‑being.

multiple-choice-1.title: Which of the following helps you approach caregiving with a healthy mindset?

options.2: Considering the situation from your and your loved one’s viewpoints
options.3: Asking for help early when you need it
options.4: Making your entire life revolve around the care recipient

correct.2: While we want to do our best for our loved ones, we cannot do this unless we are okay ourselves.
correct.3: Acknowledging your own needs, reflecting on different perspectives of caregiving and asking for help early may help you maintain a healthy mindset. As caregivers, we might tend to centre our lives around our loved one and not pursue our identities, apart from being a caregiver. This might be unhealthy in the long run.

incorrect.1: It may be worth looking more closely at your approach
incorrect.2: While we want to do our best for our loved ones, we cannot do this unless we are okay ourselves.
incorrect.3: Acknowledging your own needs, reflecting on different perspectives of caregiving and asking for help early may help you maintain a healthy mindset. As caregivers, we might tend to centre our lives around our loved one and not pursue our identities, apart from being a caregiver. This might be unhealthy in the long run.

reveal-2.locked: Reflect on what it needs for a healthy caregiving relationship to proceed.

text-11.1: Adam’s Journey Continues: From Caregiver to Mentor
text-11.2: Every caregiving journey is unique. Each person and situation shapes the experience differently.
text-11.3: Find out how Adam became a mentor for other caregivers below.

p1.1: Adam accompanied his mother for her medical appointment to see the heart specialist. She had been suffering from heart failure after a heart attack the year before.

p2.1: The doctor explained that her condition is getting worse and will likely deteriorate in the months to come.

p3.1: Adam was at a loss. He did not only have to deal with the eventuality of losing his mother but also had to take on the added responsibilities of caring for his loved one.

p4.1: He spoke to a nurse specialist, who provided him necessary resources including a support group contact. Still at a loss, Adam brought his mother home. He could not process the information …

p5.1: Over time, Adam avoided talking about end-of-life matters with his mother, even though she knew her condition was terminal. Whenever she gently tried to discuss her wishes, he pushed the conversation aside, unable to face the reality of losing her.

p6.1: Adam tried to handle his mother’s care by himself. It was not easy. There were times when Adam was frustrated juggling caregiving with his responsibilities as a parent to his children and work.

p7.1: Adam often took his frustrations out on his wife and his mother. He chose not to engage with his children as to avoid venting his frustrations on them. He starts to distance himself, fearing he may hurt his loved ones even more.

p8.1: Adam snapped at his siblings, who offered help but were unsure on what to do.

p9.1: At work, Adam lost concentration. He was reprimanded for his poor work performance.

p10.1: He sat down at a park, afraid to go home. He knew something was wrong.

text-12.2: Like Adam, many caregivers might have gone through or may be going through the same issues. Caregiving is an emotional journey with plenty of ups and downs. Many caregivers describe caregiving as a burden they must carry and account for every day.

row-2.1: Sometimes I feel like I’m living two lives – one where I care for them, and another in my head where I dream about freedom. The guilt hits hard. Every time I take a break or say ‘no’ to a task, I wonder if I’m failing them. I’ve learned to remind myself that my needs matter, too, and that taking care of myself means I can take better care of them.

She’s still here, but not really. Her smile, her laugh – the person I knew is slipping away. It feels like I’m grieving a little every day, even though she’s still sitting right next to me. I’ve learned to celebrate the small moments we still share, even as I say goodbye to the person she used to be.

There are days I feel angry – at the situation, at the world, sometimes even at them. Then I feel awful for feeling that way. I never imagined caregiving would bring so much frustration. Talking to others who’ve been through this helps. It reminds me that these feelings don’t make me a bad person – they make me human.

quote-2.quote: I struggled at the start of my caregiving journey, which is why I knew I needed coping strategies to help me find balance.

item-1.title: DEALING WITH THE PROBLEM DIRECTLY
item-1.1: Problem-focused coping strategies focus on rational solving strategies. You try to change and improve your situation by taking concrete actions and behavioural changes:

list.1:
Seek practical and financial help,
e.g. hiring paid carers, applying for financial grants, using community resources.
list.2:
Reduce time and effort,
e.g. engaging your loved one in activities, adjusting communication to avoid stress.
list.3:
Increase your sense of control
by learning about the health condition and connecting with support groups online or in person.

item-2.title: MANAGING YOUR FEELINGS
item-2.1: Emotion-focused coping strategies are generally linked to regulating your psychological and emotional distress:

list.1: Let your feelings out – talk to someone, take a time out, or even have a good cry to release tension.
list.2: Avoid too much escape or denial – try not to rely only on distractions or wishful thinking.

item-3.title: THINKING DIFFERENTLY ABOUT THE SITUATION
item-3.1: Cognitive strategies aim at coping via changing how you think about the situation:

list.1: Accepting what you can’t change – caregiving will bring challenges, and life may feel different.
list.2: Appreciating your role – remind yourself of the value you bring, keep some independence, and find meaning in your experiences.
list.3: Shifting your perspective – look for humour in tough moments and try to see the bright side when things feel hard.
list.4: Focusing on gains, not losses – see caregiving as an act of love and compassion, not as an obligation forced on you.

text-13.1: Let’s see how Adam’s caregiver journey continues.

text-98.1: Adam starts to attend a support group that meets once every month.

text-97.1: Adam is entering a new chapter of his life.

p1.1: Adam received a call from the heart failure support group. They asked if he was keen to join in their session.

p2.1: Adam sat in with the group. When he shared about his recent behaviour, he thought he would be met with judgement. Instead, everyone empathised with his situation. Adam broke down.

p3.1: He shares his personal experiences that could help other caregivers.

p4.1: At the same time, other members shared their own emotional journey with Adam, and he realised he was not alone in this. Adam started learning how to cope with his own emotions and mend the relationship with his loved ones.

p5.1: Over time, Adam started developing a mindset shift to learn how to cope with everyday caregiving needs and anticipate future challenges.

p6.1: Adam made an appointment to speak to a therapist. He understood he was dealing with anger at his helplessness in his mother’s situation. He learned techniques to better manage his emotions.

p7.1: Adam started to communicate with his loved ones on what he was going through. He was met with support and love. He took the next step in talking to his mother about her end-of-life wishes.

p8.1: Adam’s mother passed on, just like her last wish that she shared with Adam – surrounded by her loved ones.

p9.1: Adam asked himself: How do I go on after caregiving?

p10.1: He went through a period of grieving. After several months, he finally found the closure he needed.

p11.1: The support group called Adam and checked in on him. Adam shared that he would like to help others on their caregiving journey as well.

p12.1: Adam leads the support group for caregivers, sharing resources and journeying with them through their difficult times. There are also moments where he looks back to the good memories with his mother.

text-14.1: After finishing the brochure, you felt a quiet shift inside. Learning about Adam's story shows you that support is all around, and that even in difficult moments, there are ways to grow and find meaning. You begin to see caregiving not just as a duty but as a journey you can learn from.

row-2.1: Guilt can weigh heavily on caregivers, often leading to self-blame and impacting decision-making. This feeling frequently arises from the sense of not doing enough or making mistakes in the caregiving process.
Resentment can arise when caregivers feel overwhelmed and underappreciated. If left unaddressed, this anger may strain relationships and affect the caregiving environment.

header.headline: Getting to Know Singapore’s Healthcare System

p1.1: Hey! You’re ready? Let’s dive in. Joy’s story will help us to understand the Singapore Healthcare System quickly.

text-2.1: Regional Health System

row-2.1: As you may know, there are three clusters in Singapore: National University Health System (NUHS), National Healthcare Group (NHG) Singapore Health Services (SingHealth) Regional Health System.

quote-1.quote: First, we should get an overview of what types of healthcare settings exist. After that we’ll cover the types of financial assistance.

text-3.1: Overview of the Three Healthcare Settings
text-3.2: Healthcare in Singapore is delivered through public and private organisations. There are three main healthcare settings, each serving different needs and offering varying levels of care and financial support. Depending on your loved one’s condition and care needs, you may move between these settings throughout your caregiving journey.

item-1.1: Primary care is the first point of contact for patients, focusing on preventive care, health education, and management of chronic conditions through general practitioners and polyclinics.

item-2.1: Acute care is provided in hospitals for serious or urgent health issues requiring immediate medical attention, including surgeries and emergency services.

item-3.1: Community care encompasses a range of services aimed at supporting individuals in their homes or local communities, including rehabilitation, palliative care, and support for the elderly and those with chronic illnesses.

text-4.1: Stepping into the Healthcare System as a Caregiver

quote-2.quote: As a caregiver, you may have different experiences in each healthcare setting. Let’s take a look at Joy’s care journey.

text-5.1: Joy’s Experience in Primary Care Setting (GP)

slide-1.1: Joy’s mother, Siew Eng, has dementia and is on regular follow-up with a specialist. The burden of arranging for a family member to bring her mother for appointments and following up with recommendations falls on her shoulders.

slide-2.1: Siew Eng has been complaining of constant headaches and nausea. The doctor diagnosed her with hypertension and advised her to start anti-hypertensive medication with daily monitoring of her blood pressure.

slide-3.1: On top of managing Siew Eng’s challenging behaviour, Joy has to coax her to sit down for a blood pressure check and take additional medication every morning before she goes to work. Joy gets frustrated at times when Siew Eng’s dementia makes her suspicious of others.

text-6.1: Joy’s Experience in Acute Care Setting (Hospital)

p1.1: After weeks of refusing her anti-hypertensive medication, Siew Eng suffered a stroke – a serious medical emergency.

p2.1: Joy acted quickly and called an ambulance (995).

p3.1: Joy could not follow her mother into the critical care area of the A&E. She knew her mother was in good hands, but the wait took its toll on her.

p4.1: Joy’s mind spiralled into worst-case scenarios. What if her mother died or became bedridden? Had she been a good daughter?

p5.1: Joy kept asking for updates, explaining that Siew Eng has dementia.

p6.1: A nurse reassured her, and soon a doctor informed Joy that Siew Eng needed hospitalisation for further tests.

quote-3.quote: During a loved one’s emergency, experiencing fear and frustration are natural. Healthcare staff will do their best to support us and keep us updated on their care.

item-1.title: Diagnostics
item-1.1: In acute care, a range of diagnostic tests are carried out. For Siew Eng, these included CT scan and blood tests to confirm the stroke diagnosis and determine its severity.

item-2.title: Routine checks (if admitted into the wards or ICU)

list.1: Hospital routines include doctor’s rounds, monitoring vital signs, administering medication and arranging diagnostic procedures.
list.2: Doctors and nurses work together to develop individualised treatment plans based on your loved one’s condition. These plans often include medication, therapies, and ongoing monitoring.

item-3.title: The healthcare team
item-3.1: You will encounter doctors, nurses and pharmacist during your loved one’s hospitalisation. Your loved one may also be referred to other healthcare professionals if their speciality is required such as physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist, dietitian, podiatrist etc.

item-4.title: Discharge planning
item-4.1: Discharge planning is done by a multidisciplinary team. As a caregiver you might talk to doctors, nurses and other healthcare professionals. To help you get ready for discharge, there could be caregiver training to help you learn how to care for your loved one, home assessments for environmental readiness and follow-up home visits post-discharge.

text-8.1: Important Hospital Staff for Financial Matters

special-splitview-1.2: The PSA plays a vital role in assisting patients and caregivers with understanding hospital bills, national medical savings scheme and insurance claims, helping to navigate the complexities of healthcare financing. You can find them at registration counters, payment/discharge counters and the Business Office.

special-splitview-2.2: The MSW is available in hospitals to support needy patients and families facing financial difficulties. They can review your financial situation and guide you on the possible financial assistance or subsidy schemes that may be applicable for you. An inpatient referral or a walk in (in selected hospitals) consult can be done.

quote-4.quote: When your loved one is hospitalised, knowing the visiting hours and visitor limits can help you plan your visit and feel more prepared.

text-9.2: Usually, hospitals communicate with a single point of contact (POC) – sometimes called a main spokesperson – during admission. Decide who this person should be and how you’ll stay in touch.
text-9.3: In case the main contact is unavailable, hospitals may ask for a supporting contact to ensure important updates reach you promptly.
text-9.4: If you’d like to raise any concerns or stay informed, let the healthcare team know.

p1.1: After her medical treatment in the acute hospital, Siew Eng is discharged and continues her rehab in the community hospital.

text-10.1: Joy’s Experience in Community Care Setting

quote-5.quote: It was here that Joy learned community hospitals offer therapies delivered by a multi-disciplinary allied health team working with doctors and nurses to support recovery.

text-11.1: Let’s start with an overview of the common therapies you'll see.

item-1.1: Physiotherapy (PT): Helps the person to move better and become stronger. The therapist uses exercises to improve walking, balance, and overall physical movement and activity tolerance.​

item-2.1: Occupational Therapy (OT): Helps the person manage daily activities like bathing, dressing, or moving around safely. The therapist also teaches ways to adjust to their surroundings so they can be more independent.

item-3.1: Speech Therapist (ST): Helps the person with speaking, understanding others, and swallowing. The therapist uses exercises and strategies to make communicating and eating easier.

slide-1.1: After the stroke, Siew Eng completed her rehabilitation in the community hospital and is ready to go home.

slide-2.1: Joy was eager to bring her mother home, back to familiar surroundings and searched for more community services she could engage to continue her mother’s care.

slide-3.1: The rehab team spoke with Joy and her siblings about available community care services. As Siew Eng prepared to return home after completing rehabilitation, the medical social worker recommended a dementia day care programme to support her ongoing needs.

quote-6.quote: Each public hospital has an AIC Link office where caregivers can get information about community care services, programmes that provide support and documentation requirements.

back.1: Home-based Services
back.2: These are services provided in the care recipient’s home for those who are unable to access centre-based care due to mobility/accessibility issues. This allows for personalised care and support. This may include home visits by therapists, nurses or doctors, and help with daily activities like bathing.
back.3: Examples: Home Personal Care (HPC+), Home Nursing, Home Therapy.

back.1: Centre-based Services
back.2: These services take place at a centre. Senior Care Centres (SCCs) typically offer custodial day care while Active Ageing Centres (AACs) offer a variety of programmes on a drop-in basis. Both offer a range of activities for the elderly. Some SCCs offer rehabilitation sessions for seniors who require it.

back.1: Residential Care Services
back.2: When a loved one’s care needs become too much to manage at home moving to a care facility may be an option.

item-1.title: Subsidies
item-1.1: Means tested, levels of subsidies are dependent on income.

item-2.title: Medishield Life
item-2.1: Medishield Life is a healthcare insurance, primarily helps with inpatient bills, and selected outpatient treatments.

item-3.title: Medisave
item-3.1: Medisave is a savings account within CPF (Central Provident Fund) that is set aside specifically for medical purposes. The money can only be used to pay for approved medical expenses. Different withdrawal limits apply depending on the type of expense – for example, payments under the Chronic Disease Management Programme (CDMP), or for inpatient hospital bills, each have their own limits.

item-4.title: Medifund
item-4.1: Medifund provides financial assistance to help those in need pay their medical bills.

item-5.title: Flexi-Medisave

row-2.1: Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS)

text-21.1: Financial Schemes in Acute Care Setting
text-21.2: Acute care refers to treatment provided when your loved one is admitted to a hospital. Understanding the financial schemes available during this stage is crucial for caregivers. Below is a breakdown of the key components.

item-1.title: Medisave
item-1.1: Medisave is a national savings scheme that allows Singaporeans to set aside part of their income for healthcare expenses. It can be used for hospitalisation costs, outpatient treatments, and certain medical procedures.
item-1.2: Eligibility for Medisave withdrawals depends on the type of treatment and the patient’s age. Each category of treatment has specific withdrawal limits, so patients should check their Medisave balance and applicable limits before paying for treatment.

item-2.title: Medishield Life
item-2.1: Medishield Life is a basic health insurance plan that provides coverage for large hospital bills and selected outpatient treatments. It is designed to help cover the costs of hospitalisation, including room charges, surgery, and other medical expenses.
item-2.2: Patients are required to pay a portion of the bill (co-payment), and the amount covered by Medishield Life varies based on the type of ward (e.g. public or private) and the treatment received.

item-3.title: Medifund
item-3.1: Medifund is a safety net for Singaporeans who are unable to afford their medical bills even after using Medisave and Medishield Life. It provides financial to those who meet specific criteria, ensuring that no Singaporean is denied necessary medical care due to financial constraints.
item-3.2: Patients can apply for Medifund assistance through their healthcare institutions, and eligibility is assessed based on income and financial circumstances.

item-4.title: Private vs subsidised rates in the hospital
item-4.1: For subsidised care in public hospitals, you’re usually assigned a doctor by the hospital, while choosing a specific doctor is typically an option for private patients. If you choose a specific doctor, your treatment will follow the related class rates; if you later want to switch to a lower-cost option, it may require a financial assessment and approval by the hospital.

quote-11.quote: Keep in mind that subsidised rates for all types of services will be determined through means-testing.

text-25.1: Household means testing looks at your household income to decide how much government subsidy or financial help you can receive. In Singapore, this applies to primary care, acute care, and community care. Each scheme has its own subsidy limits. Generally, families with lower income receive more subsidies, while those who can afford more will pay a bit more. This helps make sure everyone can get the care they need without worrying too much about the cost!

item-1.title: More information on Means-testing
item-1.1: Means-testing evaluates the household monthly income per person based on

list.1: the number of family members (i.e. related by blood, marriage or legal adoption) staying at the same residential address as the care recipient, as indicated in their NRICs. This includes in-laws, siblings, grandchildren, uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces, cousins, step and legally adopted children, among others.
list.2: total monthly gross earnings,
list.3: for salaried employees – the average monthly employment income received over the last available 12-month period, including bonuses.
list.4: for the self-employed: (a) the monthly income derived from the last available net trade income as assessed by IRAS within the last two assessment years OR (b) the income declared to the CPF board or the income assumed under the CPF laws within the last two years.
list.5: for households with no income, the annual value of their residence will be considered instead. This situation could arise for instance, in the case of an elderly retired couple whose children have moved out into homes of their own.

item-1.2: Household means-test results are valid for 2 years.
item-1.3: If you have previously applied for any financial schemes or grants (e.g. CHAS), your means-test results could still be valid.

quote-3.quote: What helped me get the most out of my medical appointments was using these four key points:

item-1.title: 1. Prepare a list of questions
item-1.1: Here are some questions you might consider asking:

list.1: What are the next steps we need to take?
list.2: How will we know if the treatment is working? Are there any side effects?
list.3: Is there anything we should avoid doing or start doing to support our loved one?
list.4: What are the blood tests or scans for? How and when will we receive the results?

item-2.1: Keeping track of recommendations, instructions, and any important information shared during the visit, can make sharing information later easier.

item-3.title: 3. Advocate for your loved one
item-3.1: As a caregiver, part of your caregiving experience might be advocating for your loved one’s needs and preferences. Sometimes having concerns about the treatment plan is normal, feel free to share them and suggest alternatives that better reflect your loved one’s preferences.

item-4.1: It is helpful that you and your loved one have clarity about your situation. If you don’t understand something fully, don’t hesitate to ask for clarification! Verify follow-up steps, including who to contact if issues arise.

intro.heading: Reflect on your medication management.
intro.instruction: Decide whether the advice you receive as a caregiver to manage medication is helpful – or not.

1.1: Regularly review all medications to avoid confusion – check the dosage, remaining amount, expiry dates, and that the packaging is intact.

feedback.incorrect: Reviewing your medications regularly helps you stay organised and avoid dosage errors or using damaged medicine.

2.1: Avoid having more than five different medications.

feedback.incorrect: Sometimes your loved one may need more than five medications, but it’s a good idea to check with the doctor that the list is accurate.

3.1: Arrange the medications so that the ones that expire sooner are used before those that expire later.

feedback.incorrect: Organising your medication can help you save time and reduce risk of consuming expired medication.

4.1: Conduct regular checks (e. g. 3-6 months) to clear unused medications

feedback.incorrect: Regular checks are helpful to get an overview of used and unused medication.

5.1: Collect just a few months’ supply of medication even when the doctor has prescribed for 6 months.

feedback.incorrect: Yes, you don’t need to take the full supply upfront, but the best approach is to collect only what you need and then top up later using the app or arrange for delivery.

6.1: Bring a list of current medications to medical appointments and share it with your healthcare provider.

feedback.incorrect: A list can help the healthcare provider understand your medications at a glance.

7.1: Ask your doctor(s) or pharmacist to review your medication.

feedback.incorrect: Also known as medication reconciliation, reviewing the medication list helps identify issues such as duplicate doses or medicines you no longer need

quote-1.quote: Hi, :user-name:! As you probably know, many caregivers face stress. Haikal, whom I met years ago, found it so overwhelming that it affected his rest.

text-1.1: Haikal’s Experience With Caregiver Stress

item-1.title: Haikal’s story
item-1.1: A sudden stroke turns Haikal’s familiar life upside down. He struggles to care for his mom while holding everything else together. Tired and stretched thin, he reaches breaking point.
item-1.2: With Adam’s gentle guidance and support, Haikal learns new ways to cope and seek help. He realises that caregiving is not meant to be carried out alone.

text-2.1: Stress is a natural response to change and challenge. During caregiving, increased demands and limited time, energy, or support can cause stress to build up.
text-2.2: Over time, this can affect your physical and mental health, leading to fatigue, irritability, or difficulty concentrating. Recognising these signs and prioritising your well-being can help you stay calm and provide more sustainable care for your loved one.

quote-2.quote: I tried to support Haikal with his situation, and he shared this with me:

quote-3.quote: This was only the beginning. Ever since they were young, Haikal's brother, Hakim, had doubted Haikal’s choices. Now, that same constant questioning had found its way into Haikal’s caregiving decisions – making an already heavy burden feel even heavier.

p1.1: Why did you choose this hospital for our mom without discussing with me first?

p2.1: Talking to Hakim made Haikal doubt himself. Sometimes, comments from family can feel challenging, especially when things are already stressful.

p3.1: The doctor said we can try this new medication for mom and see how she responds to it, I said go ahead …
p3.2: Why was this treatment plan decided without consulting me?!

p4.1: The tension grew when Suria warmly thanked Hakim for bringing food, while Haikal’s effort went unnoticed.

p5.1: My favourite fried noodles! You’re the only one who really cares for me unlike SOMEONE else who always says "You can't eat this or that".

p6.1: The doctor already said that you have difficulty swallowing and can’t eat noodles for now. Since your other son knows you better, why don’t you let him take care of you instead?!

intro.heading: Summary of caregiver tips
intro.instruction: Decide if the tip helps you notice caregiver stress – or not.

1.1: Recognise what triggers you and where your emotional boundaries are.

feedback.incorrect: Pay attention to specific incidents or comments that trigger strong emotional reactions. Be mindfull of when you are approaching your breaking point and avoid trying to address any issues when feeling upset or angry.

Notice physical symptoms like headaches, muscle tension, or rapid heartbeat, as these are important cues that your stress is escalating. Physical signs like palpitations, tight shoulders, or fast breathing are often the first clues that your stress is rising. Haikal began noticing these signs when he argued with his brother.

3.1: Try to finish all your tasks at once so you don’t fall behind.

feedback.incorrect: Some situations feel easier to handle when we pause and take a breath first. If tasks feel too big or overwhelming, trying to handle everything at once can increase stress. Haikal learnt that breaking tasks into small, manageable steps – using bite‑sized videos to learn and simple checklists – made routine changes much easier to cope with.

Grounding techniques like the 5‑4‑3‑2‑1 method can help us to regain focus and calm during stressful moments or when your routine becomes chaotic. Haikal found this especially helpful on days he felt overloaded.

1.1: Thank you! We hope this summary exercise helped you recall tips that could benefit your day as a caregiver.

list.1: Identify what is stressing you and check if it is something within your control. While stress is normal, reacting strongly to triggers can make things feel bigger than they are.
list.2: Once you recognise the main concern, ask yourself: “Can I solve this on my own, or do I need extra help?”
list.3: It’s normal to feel emotional when things go beyond your control. Don’t be too hard on yourself when this happens.

item-2.title: Reach out for support

list.1: Call a helpline or talk to someone who can listen without judging (e.g. a trusted friend or a neighbour) to express your feelings and make sense of it.
list.2: Depending on your specific situation, you may consider calling the AIC Hotline or the national mindline for emotional support, resources and counselling options. You can find a list of various helplines on the AIC website:

item-2.link: List of helplines (opens in new tab)

item-3.title: Make informed decisions
item-3.1: When facing a big decision, give yourself time to review your options. Many caregivers make the best decision they can with the information they have at that point in time.
item-3.2: What matters most is your intention. Each experience helps you grow more confident in future decisions.

list.1: Engage in activities you enjoy that help you recharge, such as going for a walk, doing a hobby, or getting some exercise.
list.2: Make sleep a priority – it’s essential for your well-being and often overlooked.
list.3: Meditation or prayer can help you slow down, find calm, and create a moment just for yourself.
list.4: Create a designated calm space for times when you feel stressed or triggered – for example, when your loved one’s behaviour becomes emotionally difficult to manage.
list.5: It can be challenging to find time for yourself, especially when everything feels overwhelming. But even small moments of rest can make a meaningful difference.

quote-5.quote: Here’s one last idea that may help you manage future stress. Think about the most stressful day you had as a caregiver ...

row-2.1: … and now, look back at the day Haikal had. What would you do differently with the knowledge you have now?
Remember that you made it through that difficult day. That already shows your strength.

text-2.1: Have a look at the different areas below where caregivers may struggle with.

item-1.title: Physical health – Taking care of your own body

quote-1.1: Welcome back, :user-name:! Caregiving isn’t only about the physical actions you take. Effective communication will make your life as a caregiver a lot easier.

row-1.1: This was something Sumitha, a friend whom I met at one of the self-help group sessions, had to learn early in her caregiving journey. Let me tell you her story - it might help you as well.

text-1.1: Sumitha’s Story

slide-1.1: Kumar, Sumitha’s husband, was a police officer for most of his life until his retirement.

slide-2.1: Prior to Kumar’s retirement, he and Sumitha enjoyed spending quality time together, often going to the beach for a stroll.

slide-3.1: After he retired, he started to have difficulties in managing his diabetes as he did not follow old routines anymore.

slide-4.1: Eventually he suffered complications from the uncontrolled diabetes which resulted in a right below knee amputation.

slide-5.1: Kumar struggled with accepting his new role, limitations and routines.

heading-1.1: Something Changed Between Sumitha and Kumar

p1.1: We need to keep monitoring your sugar ...
p1.2: I will have to go back to work now, we need some spare cash, and we should not trouble the children ...
p1.3: I will be getting a helper, have done the interview and though she doesn’t speak our language, she is experienced in caring for a senior ...

p2.1: Kumar kept quiet and did not listen. He usually wasn’t given a chance to talk and kept his thoughts to himself, even though it bothered him that their lives seemed to revolve around him and his medical problems.

p3.1: I miss my wife and the time we spent together doing things we both like.

p4.1: One day, tensions finally boiled over. Kumar repeatedly called Sumitha while she was at work.

p5.1: Why is there someone from a maid agency standing at our door?!

p6.1: I need you to come home immediately! I don’t want a helper!

p7.1: You don’t even appreciate all I have done for you ...

quote-2.1: Communication is not only about talking to your loved ones.

text-2.1: It also involves understanding body language, choosing the right moment to start a conversation, and interacting effectively with healthcare professionals or Migrant Domestic Workers (MDWs). This chapter covers two key scenarios: involving your loved one in care decisions and communicating with your MDW.

heading-2.1: Involving Your Loved One in Care Decisions

p1.1: Sumitha was finding it harder to care for Kumar on her own. She mentioned the idea of hiring an MDW a few times, but Kumar wasn’t open to it and didn’t participate in the discussions.

p2.1: When Lusi, the MDW finally started work, Kumar felt that things were moving too fast. He didn't feel fully included in the decisions made about his care, and this upset him.

p4.1: Because he wasn’t properly involved earlier, Kumar felt his privacy and control slipping away. These feelings built up, and their conversations quickly turned into arguments.

multiple-choice-1.title: What do you think made Sumitha and Kumar upset with each other?

options.1: Sumitha didn’t involve her loved one in the care decision.
options.2: Kumar still wants to decide for himself and be involved in choices that affect his day-to-day life. He didn't feel like Sumitha had considered his wishes.
options.3: Sumitha was too busy with work to attend to Kumar.
options.4: Sumitha did not pay attention to Kumar’s reactions, including his adverse body language, when she brought up the idea of hiring an MDW.

correct.2: It is important to involve your loved one in care decisions as much as possible, respect their feelings, and understand their personality and preferences – including their love language – to build a better connection. (You will learn more about love languages later.)

incorrect.2: It is important to involve your loved one in care decisions as much as possible, respect their feelings, and understand their personality and preferences – including their love language – to build a better connection. (You will learn more about love languages later.)

quote-3.1: When I spoke to Sumitha about this, it became clear that she and Kumar were not communicating effectively.

back.1: Acceptance of relationship dynamic changes: Sumitha’s role changed from being Kumar’s spouse to being his caregiver, but the couple never talked about what that would mean for them.
back.2: Readiness for conversation: On one hand, Sumitha didn’t engage with Kumar’s wishes and overlooked his negative reactions to her idea of hiring an MDW. On the other hand, Kumar didn’t express his feelings and doubts clearly until the situation escalated.

heading-3.1: Alternative Approach That Could Have Worked Better

row-1.1: Although Sumitha and Kumar worked things out later, the misunderstanding could have been prevented. Let’s go back to the moment before Lusi was hired and imagine how better communication could have helped.

slide-1.1: One day, after Kumar and Sumitha returned from a medical appointment, Sumitha started thinking about future changes to their lives.

slide-2.1: She approached Kumar and initiated a conversation about long-term care plans as she felt that she couldn't keep up with holding a full-time job, doing the housework and worrying about Kumar being along at home.

slide-3.1: She discussed the need for assistance at home and someone to help Kumar when he needed it.

slide-4.1: And she shared her life plans and concerns for Kumar's safety as well as the potential need for an MDW.

quote-4.1: This was a better start, because Sumitha shared her worries with Kumar. Effective communication means to consider the worries and points of view (POV) of everyone.

item-1.1: Sumitha started working to support the family. This meant that Kumar would be alone at home for most of the day.
item-1.2: She also started making plans to ensure that Kumar could focus on managing his medical needs. Not managing his diabetes already caused him a lot of inconveniences.
item-1.3: Sumitha had been feeling tired and knew she’d be unable to continually support Kumar alone but did not share this with him initially.

item-2.1: Kumar wanted to support Sumitha in her decision making but felt like a burden to her. He also wanted to do things independently to lessen the load on her.
item-2.2: He saw having a helper as losing opportunities to talk and interact with Sumitha.
item-2.3: He felt that their relationship now only centred around the tasks related to his care and felt disconnected from Sumitha.
item-2.4: He felt uncomfortable having someone other than his wife, help him with private activities of daily living such as showering.

heading-4.1: How Considering Both POVs Would Have Changed the Situation

quote-5.1: Involving Kumar from the beginning gives him the opportunity to address his concerns and makes collaborative decision-making possible.

slide-1.1: Kumar expresses his preference for Sumitha to continue taking care of him, especially with private activities like showering.

slide-2.1: Sumitha listens to Kumar and honestly expresses her own fears of not being able to cope ...

slide-3.1: ... especially with transfers and showering and reassures him about comfort and independence.

slide-4.1: Sumitha and Kumar engage in dialogue, exploring options together, and Kumar becomes more agreeable to hiring an MDW.

slide-5.1: Kumar finally admits that he worries that a helper would take away the time he spends with Sumitha – something that is very important to him.

slide-6.1: Sumitha realises that activities outside of caregiving matter to Kumar and they start to spend time the way the used to.

text-3.1: People give and receive love differently. Kumar’s preference to spend meaningful time with Sumitha is an expression of what is called a “love language”. You’ll learn more about it after a few final tips for effective communication.

item-1.title: OPEN COMMUNICATION IS NEEDED FROM BOTH PARTIES
item-1.1: Explore, together:
item-1.3: How can we work together to support each other?
item-1.4: What are our fears and frustrations?

item-2.title: ELEMENTS OF EFFECTIVE COMMUNICATION
item-2.1: Communication often isn’t easy. These elements can help make it easier:
item-2.2: Active listening: eye contact, non-verbal cues, reflect/paraphrase, avoid interruption
item-2.3: Clear communication: speak in an appropriate pace, break down complex information, ask for feedback
item-2.4: Empathy/Compassion: show genuine interest, validate emotions, use supportive language, reassure and encourage

item-3.title: NON-VERBAL CUES
item-3.1: Body language matters. Facial expressions and body language tell us how a person may be feeling such as nervousness, being upset or anxious (e.g. fidgeting, having arms crossed, pacing).
item-3.2: Non-verbal cues: look out for eye contact, facial expressions, their posture, gestures, proximity, touch

p1.1: Shortly after Sumitha hired Lusi, the situation escalated. Sumitha was preparing for work, when she heard shouting from the bathroom.

item-2.1: Communication often isn’t easy. These elements can help make it easier:
item-2.2: Active listening: eye contact, non-verbal cues, reflect/paraphrase, avoid interruption

item-2.4: Empathy/Compassion: show genuine interest, validate emotions, use supportive language, reassure and encourage

header.title: Ways Your Loved One Feel Loved and Supported

text-1.1: Involving your loved one in care decisions is easier when they feel understood and valued. Different people value different expressions of love – including older adults receiving care. Understanding their love language helps you express care in ways that resonate with them. Loved ones can support these discussions by sharing their preferences, voicing concerns early, and asking questions to help make care planning more collaborative and less stressful.

back.1: Words of Affirmation
back.2: Offering verbal encouragement, compliments, and appreciation can uplift and reassure your loved one.
back.4: You mean so much to me.
back.6: I appreciate how strong you’ve been – it hasn’t been easy.

back.1: Acts of Service
back.2: Show care by helping in ways that make life easier for them.
back.5: Helping with daily tasks like organising medication.

back.1: Quality Time
back.2: Spending meaningful moments together.
back.3: For example, this could be as simple as sitting together and sharing stories, watching a favourite show, or looking through old photos.

back.1: Physical Touch
back.2: Providing comfort through gentle, caring touch.
back.4: Holding their hand during difficult moments.
back.5: Giving a gentle hug when they feel anxious.

back.1: Receiving Gifts
back.2: Giving thoughtful presents to show you care.
back.4: Bringing a small treat they enjoy.
back.5: Giving a cozy blanket or a handwritten note.

text-2.1: You might ask, how can you know your loved one’s love language – have a look at the following tips.
text-2.2: Observe what they appreciate most: Do they light up when you praise them, spend time together, or help with chores?
text-2.3: Notice what they ask for: “Can you sit with me?” suggests quality time; “Can you help me with this?” points to acts of service.
text-2.4: Pay attention to what they do for others: Often, people express love in the way they want to receive it.
text-2.5: Ask gently: “What makes you feel most cared for?”
text-2.6: Share your own love language: Let your loved one know what makes you feel cared for. When you express your needs clearly, it helps them understand how they can show love in a way that matters to you.

header.title: Helpful Tips on How to Communicate With MDWs

item-1.title: USE TOOLS TO OVERCOME LANGUAGE BARRIERS
item-1.1: Leverage translation apps (e.g. Google Translate) or pictorial guides for daily tasks.
item-1.2: Create simple checklists in both languages to avoid confusion and come to an agreement.

item-2.title: PLAN AND PRIORITISE CARE TASKS
item-2.1: Break down tasks so the MDW knows what to focus on.
item-2.2: Be realistic – one MDW cannot care for a senior, babysit young children, and manage all housework at the same time.
item-2.3: Clarify which tasks the MDW should prioritise, and which tasks you and your family members will continue to handle.

item-3.title: ENSURE SAFETY DURING CARE ACTIVITIES
item-3.1: Use assistive devices during transfers (e.g. transfer belt, back support) whenever needed to keep both the MDW and your loved one safe.
item-3.2: Learn proper techniques so you can supervise how the MDW assist in your loved one’s daily activities to reduce risk of falls or strain.

item-4.title: ACKNOWLEDGE CAREGIVER FATIGUE AND SHOW APPRECIATION
item-4.1: Recognise that caring for a senior is physically and emotionally demanding.
item-4.2: Encourage MDWs to take sufficient breaks and practice self-care.
item-4.3: Regularly acknowledge the efforts of MDWs.
item-4.4: Simple words like “Thank you for taking care of [name]” can boost morale.

item-5.title: USE SIMPLE LANGUAGE AND SHORT SENTENCES
item-5.1: Speak slowly and clearly, focusing on one subject at a time.
item-5.2: Avoid jargon; use familiar words and repeat key points if needed.

item-6.title: MANAGING EMERGENCIES
item-6.1: Provide MDWs with a clear emergency plan, including who to call first (family, ambulance).
item-6.2: Keep emergency numbers visible and accessible.
item-6.3: Consider sending them for training to increase their capability in caring for your loved one.
item-6.4: Be realistic on the limitations of the MDW. A single person often is unable to care for an elderly, babysit younger children and do all the housework.

header.title: How Ageing and Health Conditions Affect Communication

item-1.title: Why is communication sometimes difficult?
item-1.1: Ageing, stroke or dementia can affect how a person hears, sees, thinks, or finds words.

item-2.title: Does this mean my loved one is not listening?
item-2.1: No. They may want to respond but struggle to understand or express themselves.
item-2.2: Regularly check if your loved one’s vision and hearing need support – such as glasses, hearing aids, or adjustments in the environment – to ensure they can stay engaged and feel understood.

item-3.title: What can I do to help?
item-3.1: Check that glasses or hearing aids are used.
item-3.2: Reduce background noise and face them when speaking.

item-4.title: What should I avoid?
item-4.1: Avoid rushing or talking over them.
item-4.2: Avoid speaking about them as if they are not there.
